national.title: She went to college to become a social worker. Now she's joined the skilled trades
national.summary: While the rise of AI continues to fuel the debate over whether college is worth the cost, apprenticeships in the skilled trades are having a moment, drawing in people of all backgrounds including college graduates.
national.body:
Ashley Baukman is an apprentice at The Electrical Trades Center in Columbus, Ohio. With the future of work uncertain, some college graduates are turning to the skilled trades for job security. Andrew Spear for NPR hide caption

COLUMBUS, Ohio — A few miles south of The Ohio State University, Ashley Baukman is wrestling with a piece of steel tubing, using only a manual tool called a foot pedal and her sheer strength to bend it 90 degrees.

This class in conduit bending at The Electrical Trades Center of Central Ohio is part of an apprenticeship program Baukman began in the spring. She's here in class one day out of every two weeks. Other days, she's out on construction sites, working under the supervision of journeymen electricians.

For the 36-year-old college graduate and licensed social worker, it's a new chapter — one she hopes will be the foundation of a long-term career.

Being the first in her family to graduate from college had been a point of pride for Baukman.

"I was like, 'Oh, I'm going to do this. I'm going to do it the right way,'" she says. "But it didn't really work out that way, and that's okay. You live and you learn."

Baukman bends steel tubing alongside other apprentices at The Electrical Trades Center, a training school that's funded through the collective bargaining agreement between the Central Ohio Chapter of the National Electrical Contractors Association and the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 683. Andrew Spear for NPR hide caption

Now, as an apprentice, she's getting paid just over $25 an hour for time on the job and a stipend for days she's in class. Already, she's earning more than she was as a social worker and is set to nearly double her wage in just over three years. So far, she's finding the work engaging and rewarding.

national.title: This teen had no place to go, so a hospital became his home
national.summary: A young survivor of gun violence lived on the third floor of a St. Louis children's hospital, moving through the halls in a wheelchair, on and off for over three years. He said it became his home when he had nowhere safe to go.
national.body: St. Louis — The teen's hospital stay began in room 3005.The room didn't feel like home at first. Back then, Jaloni didn't have posters on the wall or snacks on the shelf, and he hadn't learned about the morgue yet.He just wanted to survive. Fresh gunshot wounds filled the 14-year-old's body with unbearable pain. That first night, Jaloni said, he could barely move.But in his own way, Jaloni could fly. His pain medication was so strong that the teenager said he felt like he was soaring in a dream.In reality, though, Jaloni was a teenager caught between two worlds. Around his friends he had been a fearless risk-taker who knew how to steal without getting caught. Inside the hospital, Jaloni was now a boy who needed his grandmother to tell him that everything would be OK and that somehow life would get better as soon as he was released from the hospital.But she couldn't make that promise. No one could.He ended up staying in the SSM Health Cardinal Glennon Children's Hospital for more than 475 days over the next three years, his medical records show. Some of that time was not because he needed the hospital's medical care but because he had no safe place to go. The now-18-year-old asked KFF Health News to use only nicknames or first names to protect his family's safety.Like thousands of children throughout the country, Jaloni experienced what is called a social stay. The practice also known as hospital boarding, in which children remain in hospitals "beyond medical necessity," has become a costly and intractable issue nationwide.A shortage of suitable foster care homes can mean children with mental health issues, chronic physical conditions, or disabilities that require special accommodations get stuck in hospitals. One study from Minnesota found that boarding a child with a complex medical condition in a hospital cost about $3,932 a day in 2017.It is not clear how much of Jaloni's hospitalization was beyond what was medically necessary or how much those extra days in the hospital cost. national.title: Trump in Asia for Putin, Xi summit; possible Kim meeting
national.summary: The president arrived in Manila for the start of a multi-day swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping in a highly anticipated summit. He says he may also meet with North Korea's Kim Jong Un.
national.body: President Trump arrived in the Philippines Tuesday to start a multiday swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping for a highly anticipated summit later this week. Ahead of his departure from Washington Monday, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China.The meeting between Mr. Trump, Xi and Putin, which marks the first among the three leaders, is expected to center on decreasing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the White House said, and comes as the wars in Iran and Ukraine remain in focus.Mr. Trump said Monday they would discuss denuclearization, which he called a "tough subject," as well as Iran and Ukraine, although an official said over the weekend that Ukraine was not expected to be discussed. In Manila, the president will attend the annual Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. He will meet with leaders of Japan, India and Australia on security in the Indo-Pacific on Tuesday. He's also scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a dinner with leaders of the Southeast Asian nations and other regional leaders, the White House said. On Wednesday, the president is set to hold a state visit and lunch banquet with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos at the presidential palace, before departing for Shenzhen, China. There, he'll meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with APEC leaders, and on Thursday, hold the meeting with Putin and Xi.Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is expected to join the president on the trip, according to a senior White House official, but will not be part of the meeting with Putin and Xi.Mr. Trump's trip to Asia comes after he visited China in May for a summit with Xi, where he touted making "fantastic trade deals" and acknowledged a shared desire to end the U.S.-Iran conflict. national.title: Russia downs over 1,400 Ukrainian drones as Kyiv hits a key bridge in Crimea
national.summary: Ukraine's forces targeted a key rail and road bridge between Russia and the Crimean Peninsula for a second day. Moscow's forces, meanwhile, fired ballistic missiles and drones at Kyiv.
national.body:
FILE - A freight train runs on rails of a railway link of the Crimean Bridge connecting Russian mainland and Crimean peninsula over the Kerch Strait not far from Kerch, Crimea, on Monday, July 17, 2023. AP Photo//AP hide caption

Russian air defenses downed more than 1,400 Ukrainian drones during a second straight night of massive attacks, Russia's Defense Ministry said Tuesday, as Ukraine's forces targeted a key rail and road bridge between Russia and the Crimean Peninsula for a second day.

Moscow's forces, meanwhile, fired ballistic missiles and drones at Kyiv, hitting two of the Ukrainian capital's main bridges and killing at least two people.

The apparent escalation in aerial attacks came as Russia and Ukraine await a date for the next round of U.S.-mediated talks aimed at ending the war that began with Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor on Feb. 24, 2022.

On Monday, Russia said that it downed 1,336 Ukrainian drones in the highest number of interceptions it had reported so far during the war. On Tuesday, Russia said that it downed 1,441 Ukrainian drones.

Also Monday, Ukraine targeted the huge Kerch Bridge, a crucial span for moving military and civilian supplies from Russia to Crimea that is also a potent symbol of Russia's illegal annexation of the peninsula in 2014. Officials said that the damage then was insignificant.

But unconfirmed media reports said that Tuesday's repeat attack on the bridge severely damaged one of its two arches. The Associated Press couldn't immediately verify reports that a span of the bridge collapsed.

The Russian-installed governor of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said that traffic across the bridge has been halted and urged people "to refrain from trips in the direction of the bridge." He didn't mention any damage.

national.title: Crimea bridge shut after Ukrainian strike, as Russia hits Kyiv crossings
national.summary: The bridge linking Crimea and Russia has reportedly sustained major damage, while two routes through Kyiv are closed.
national.body:
A key bridge linking occupied Crimea and Russia is closed after a Ukrainian strike inflicted major damage on the prized Kremlin asset.

Images shared by Ukrainian officials showed a section of the Crimean Bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - had collapsed into the water.

Russian officials confirmed the structure had been damaged by drones, while Russia's deputy prime minister was due to chair an emergency meeting to discuss the situation.

Meanwhile, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, both important crossings over the Dnipro River, were closed after Russia targeted the Ukrainian capital overnight.

Former Ukrainian adviser Anton Gerashchenko shared images and video footage appearing to show extensive damage to the road section of the Crimea bridge, with remnants of the support arch and road section seen protruding from the water below.

The bridge, which has come under repeated attack by Ukrainian forces, was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2018.

While Ukraine has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the Crimea bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Putin.

The timing of the Crimea bridge strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This strike could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.

national.title: Indian woman gang-raped while pregnant in 2002 'heartbroken' after two perpetrators bailed
national.summary: Bilkis Bano has spoken of her "pain, shock and disbelief" at the top court order and vowed to fight back.
national.body:
The article has details that some readers may find disturbing

A pregnant Muslim woman who was gang-raped and saw 14 family members murdered during the 2002 Gujarat riots has spoken of her "pain, shock and disbelief" after two of her rapists were recently granted bail.

Bilkis Bano said in a statement that she heard about the top court order through press reports and vowed to fight back.

The freed men are from a group of 11 convicts - part of a Hindu mob - serving life terms for the attack on Bano.

All the men were also freed in 2022 after a Gujarat government order. That decision, and the celebrations as they left prison, caused global outrage . In 2024, the Supreme Court overturned the order .

In a short three-page order dated 28 October, the Supreme Court granted bail to Bipinchand Kanaiyalal Joshi and Pradip Ramanlal Modhiya and suspended their sentences while their petition challenging a 2017 Bombay High Court order is being heard.

The judges explained that the early release was because the two convicts "have been under incarceration for a period of more than 17 years" and "that one of the appellants has a severe handicap".

On Tuesday, Bano's lawyer Shobha Gupta told the BBC that the news of Joshi and Modhiya's release had left "Bilkis heartbroken".

national.title: Mozambique opposition leader faces trial over deadly 2024 election unrest
national.summary: Venâncio Mondlane faces several charges over 2024 post-election protests that left hundreds of people dead.
national.body:
Tensions are running high in Mozambique's capital, Maputo, with a heavy police deployment as a prominent opposition leader goes on trial over deadly protests that followed the country's disputed 2024 elections.

Venâncio Mondlane faces several charges, including incitement to terrorism and civil disobedience, over protests that left hundreds of people dead. He denies any wrongdoing.

Security has been tightened around the Supreme Court, where Mondlane is due to appear on Tuesday, with authorities fearing a fresh wave of demonstrations by his supporters.

Police have appealed to citizens to follow the proceedings calmly and avoid actions that could threaten public order.

The trial is widely seen as a major test of Mozambique's political stability, nearly two years after disputed elections triggered some of the country's deadliest political unrest in decades.

"The trial is a real test for Mozambique. It is is an important opportunity to demonstrate that the rule of law applies equally to everyone," said Luis Nhachote, a political analyst.

Mondlane, who challenged the presidential election results that declared Daniel Chapo of the ruling Frelimo party the winner, accused the authorities of widespread electoral fraud and called for nationwide protests and work stoppages.

national.title: Nigerians among 12 suspects arrested in $4.5m Canada luxury car theft syndicate
national.summary: Canadian authorities say they have recovered 96 luxury vehicles destined for West Africa.
national.body:
Canadian police have arrested 12 suspects, including eight Nigerians, in an investigation into an alleged car theft syndicate.

They are accused of stealing luxury vehicles and shipping them to West Africa.

Police in Peel, Ontario said they had recovered 96 high-value vehicles concealed in shipping containers. The vehicles, valued at $4.5m (£3.4m) were destined for export via Canadian ports.

The trafficking of vehicles from North America and Europe to African countries has been a long-standing concern for law enforcement agencies.

The suspects face 231 charges, with arrest warrants issued for others. Police say some of the accused may face deportation after their criminal proceedings are concluded.

The arrests followed months of what police described as an "extensive auto theft investigation".

The investigations began in March in partnership with Canada's border agency after police identified a warehouse allegedly being used to store stolen vehicles.

Investigators believe the network was led by five people who coordinated the theft, transportation and export of the stolen vehicles, with the others playing supporting roles.

national.title: Japan sends up jets after alleged Russian incursion of its airspace
national.summary: Taiwan and South Korea also responded to Russian military aircraft detected near their airspaces.
national.body:
Japan says it launched fighter jets and "strongly" protested after two suspected Russian aircraft violated its airspace early on Tuesday.

South Korea also says it deployed fighter jets, while Taiwan says it "responded" to Russian military aircraft detected in their respective air defence identification zones.

These are unofficial buffer areas beyond territorial airspace where governments identify approaching aircraft for security purposes. Moscow has yet to comment.

The alleged incursions are a reminder of Russia's military power ahead of the Apec economic summit in China this week, which Vladimir Putin will attend alongside US President Donald Trump.

Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the flight paths of the Russian aircraft, off the south-western Okinoshima island, were a "serious infringement of Japan's sovereignty" and "completely unacceptable".

The last such incursion was in 2024, when a Russian military patrol plane entered Japanese airspace off Rebun island, Hokkaido.

Taiwan says its military "responded accordingly" after two Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone, also on Tuesday.

South Korea says it sent up jets after an unspecified number of Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone over the Sea of Japan. The aircraft departed without violating South Korean airspace, authorities said.

national.title: Body of Melbourne Cup horse found dumped in Sydney skip
national.summary: The remains of a top Australian racehorse that died of colic on Monday were found at a public rubbish tip.
national.body:
The body of a top Australian racehorse has been found dumped in a skip bin, hours after its trainer revealed the horse had died from colic.

In a video shared online, only two weeks after So You Are raced in the Melbourne Cup, the deceased racehorse appeared to be lying in a large metal bin surrounded by other household rubbish in Sydney.

Trainer Bjorn Baker - who shared news of the horse's death from colic on Monday - has said he was "deeply distressed" by the video, and called for a "full explanation".

Racing NSW, the state's industry regulator, said a preliminary investigation had found the horse was later properly buried, but called the way its body was handled "completely unacceptable".

"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said in an statement shared online.

"He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death."

So You Are had a successful run during spring, winning four times at respected races including the Rosehill, Randwick and the Bendigo Cup.

The five-year-old recently finished eight in the Melbourne Cup, which was won by Point of Law, a horse previously owned by King Charles III.

national.title: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72
national.summary: Efforts to recover bodies after a “double-tap” attack in southern Ukraine are being hampered by continuing Russian strikes, officials say.
national.body:
Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.

Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.

Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site.

The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there were multiple Russian strikes during the rescue.

The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged during the operation, which has now concluded.

With the DSNS saying the death toll had risen to at least 72 people, the attack on Komyshuvakha has become the second deadliest single incident of the Ukraine war.

Oleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".

He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.

national.body: Manila, Philippines — Protests against President Trump's visit to the Philippines have popped up around the country, as local residents criticize a Trump administration project to build an artificial intelligence and manufacturing hub just north of the country's capital of Manila. In the opening salvo for Pax Silica, a U.S. State Department-led international initiative to secure non-Chinese supply chains for high-tech manufacturing, a more than 4,000-acre manufacturing hub is planned to be built in the Philippines.Protesters in Manila on Monday held signs reading "Trump Out," drawings of him as a clown or a devil, and signs calling on the public to reject the Pax Silica initiative.Critics argue the proposed industrial hub will displace farming communities and the Indigenous Aeta tribe, harm the country's water supply and represent U.S. imperialism over the Philippines. "They have been grabbing our lands. They have been grabbing our economy. … Pax Silica is just for the U.S. It's not for us," said Maninging Vilog, a teacher and advocate for Aeta communities."If you look at the farmers, what do they care about AI? The people selling water … selling cigarettes, the people who drive buses. What do they care about AI?" said Kaiser Cortina, a 20-year-old protester. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., also a subject of the protests this week, supports the hub. He said in October he is "terribly excited" about the project's economic benefits, framing it as a "grand opportunity" for the country to move up the "value chain" by shifting into advanced manufacturing and research, according to PhilStar Global. Marcos' administration has claimed the project could create 100,000 to 130,000 jobs. Over 25 countries have signed on to the Pax Silica initiative since it was announced by the U.S. State Department in December 2025, including the United Kingdom, Israel, Japan and India. national.title: Vance says he will decide 'sometime next year' about 2028 US presidential run
national.summary: The US vice-president tells Fox News that when he makes a decision to run or otherwise, he will "be all in on whatever that decision is".
national.body:
US Vice-President JD Vance has said he will make a decision "sometime next year" about whether or not he will run for president in 2028.

In an interview with Fox News, Vance would not provide a timeline on making a determination, but signaled he is not in a hurry to make up his mind.

"I haven't made a decision. We'll figure it out sometime next year," Vance said. When pressed by host Laura Ingraham, he added: "When I make a decision, I'll be all in on whatever that decision is."

The comments came amid growing interest in Vance's next moves in the weeks since voters handed both President Donald Trump and Republicans a resounding defeat in the midterm elections.

People in Vance's orbit who have spoken to the BBC said the November elections did not change the timeline around his decision-making process for 2028. He is expected to run but allies believe he could wait several months to make a final decision.

Speculation about Vance's White House aspirations began the moment President Trump selected him as his 2024 running mate. The pick positioned Vance, who entered the White House as one of the youngest vice-presidents in US history, as the most likely heir to Trump's Make America Great Again (Maga) movement.

But while serving in office, Vance has carefully avoided discussing his own political ambitions.

He kept that up during the midterms, when supporters frequently interrupted his campaign speeches to urge him to run in 2028. Vance's stock response was that Republicans needed to focus on the election at hand in November.

national.title: Trump says Alaska voters chose the wrong Dan Sullivan. What does the data show?
national.summary: Votes are still being counted in the Alaska Senate race, with Democrat Mary Peltola ahead of Republican incumbent Senator Dan S Sullivan.
national.body:
Almost two weeks after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterm elections, votes are still being counted in the race to elect a senator in Alaska, with Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ahead of her Republican rival - Senator Dan S Sullivan.

This Senate contest has drawn scrutiny after another Dan Sullivan entered the race earlier this year - with ballot papers listing both the incumbent Dan S Sullivan and a Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

Republicans have said this could have confused voters, prompting an unsuccessful legal challenge and President Donald Trump claiming votes for "the fake Dan Sullivan" were supposed to be for "the real Dan Sullivan".

US media has not forecasted a winner in the race - the last Senate seat still without a winner after the 3 November election.

But with 98% of the vote counted, even if Senator Dan S Sullivan's votes were combined with Daniel J Sullivan Jr's votes, this would still not overcome Peltola's lead.

Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can vote for five candidates in order of preference. If no candidate reaches more than 50% of the first preference votes, then voters' other choices will be used to decide who wins.

BBC Verify has analysed voting data showing voters' second choices. It shows that over a third of voters who put Daniel J Sullivan Jr first left their second choice blank.

The next highest second-choice preference was for the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola - receiving nearly twice as many second-choice votes as the Republican Dan S Sullivan.

national.summary: Votes are still being counted in the Alaska Senate race, with Democrat Mary Peltola ahead of Republican incumbent Senator Dan S Sullivan.
national.body:
Almost two weeks after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterm elections, votes are still being counted in the race to elect a senator in Alaska, with Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ahead of her Republican rival - Senator Dan S Sullivan.

This Senate contest has drawn scrutiny after another Dan Sullivan entered the race earlier this year - with ballot papers listing both the incumbent Dan S Sullivan and a Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

Republicans have said this could have confused voters, prompting an unsuccessful legal challenge and President Donald Trump claiming votes for "the fake Dan Sullivan" were supposed to be for "the real Dan Sullivan".

US media has not forecasted a winner in the race - the last Senate seat still without a winner after the 3 November election.

But with 98% of the vote counted, even if Senator Dan S Sullivan's votes were combined with Daniel J Sullivan Jr's votes, this would still not overcome Peltola's lead.

Alaska uses a ranked-choice voting system, which means voters can vote for five candidates in order of preference. If no candidate reaches more than 50% of the first preference votes, then voters' other choices will be used to decide who wins.

BBC Verify has analysed voting data showing voters' second choices. It shows that over a third of voters who put Daniel J Sullivan Jr first left their second choice blank.

The next highest second-choice preference was for the Democratic candidate Mary Peltola - receiving nearly twice as many second-choice votes as the Republican Dan S Sullivan.

national.title: Nvidia dismisses 'Bring Jensen Back' campaign as Trump backs effort to reinstate ex boss
national.summary: A number of tech figures have backed an effort asking the AI chip giant to give Jensen Huang his job back.
national.body:
Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for the company's co-founder Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, supported the effort.

Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, joining a list of supporters including SpaceX's Elon Musk who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign.

But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in reinstating him after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs , including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy.

The same day, the White House also said it will further restrict China's access to AI chips from firms like Nvidia.

The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance.

Since Huang's departure, more than 175,000 people have signed an open letter calling for the board to reinstate the tech billionaire while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.

Major tech bosses, including Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return.

national.title: Imran Khan seeks urgent medical care fearing he 'may not return alive'
national.summary: Pakistan's ex-prime minister, who has been in prison since August 2023, says he has been denied justice.
national.body:
Pakistan's jailed former PM Imran Khan has appealed for urgent medical treatment, saying that his and his wife's health has been deteriorating.

"At 74, this unrelenting state is taking me to a place from which I may not return alive," the cricket star-turned-politician wrote in a letter published by his lawyer Salman Safdar.

Authorities in Islamabad maintain that Khan gets seen weekly by doctors, who have assessed that he is of "satisfactory" health.

Khan, who faces more than 100 charges, has been in prison since August 2023. His wife Bushra Bibi was jailed along with him last year. Khan argues the cases against them, ranging from corruption to selling state gifts, are politically motivated.

Concerns over Khan's health have grown louder in the past year, with his family claiming he has lost most of his vision in his right eye after prison authorities failed to take action.

In his letter, Khan wrote that doctors have told him he is "highly vulnerable to a brain haemorrhage and cardiac arrest", and that his heart has already "suffered damage".

He also expressed concern for Bushra Bibi, whom he says suffered a detached retina in April and underwent surgery in secrecy. Khan said he fears she may lose her sight without further surgery.

"I have fought impossible legal battles in countless cases, and I have not stopped. But the system has stopped giving me justice," he wrote.

national.body: United Airlines said it has resolved a "widespread system outage" it was dealing with Monday afternoon, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network prompted a nationwide ground stop."We have resolved a technology issue that delayed flight departures," the airline said Monday evening. "While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights." The outage lasted about 90 minutes.Earlier, United said it was "troubleshooting a technology issue affecting departing flights."A memo from the union representing United Airlines pilots indicated the issue was with the airline's weight and balance calculation system, noting: "The Company cannot provide outbound flights with final weights." A United spokesperson said there's no indication the outage was related to a cybersecurity issue. The flight tracking website FlightAware showed United with 715 delayed flights late Monday afternoon, although it was unclear how many of those were the result of the short-lived tech issue. About an hour and a half after the outage was resolved, it didn't appear that the brief outage was having a major impact on the carrier's flights, with delays and cancellations roughly in line with its competitors.The disruption for the Chicago-based carrier came less than 24 hours after the Federal Aviation Administration said airline schedules across the U.S. were returning to normal following Friday's hourslong ground stop. The United computer problem was just the latest high-profile technology meltdown. Earlier in the day, thousands of people reported being unable to access their online accounts at several major U.S. banks after JPMorgan Chase had a technical problem. On Friday, the FAA ordered every U.S. flight grounded because a new router that was installed malfunctioned and overwhelmed the aging air traffic control system. national.title: Trump appeals to state and federal courts to erase hush money criminal conviction
national.summary: A federal appeals court is weighing whether it can — or should — intervene in President Donald Trump's hush money case now that a New York State appellate court has heard arguments in his quest to erase the historic conviction.
national.body:
Michael R. Sisak, Associated Press Michael R. Sisak, Associated Press

NEW YORK (AP) — A federal appeals court is weighing whether it can — or should — intervene in President Donald Trump's hush money case now that a New York State appellate court has heard arguments in his quest to erase the historic conviction.

A three-judge panel of the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Monday spent more than an hour questioning Trump's lawyer and a state prosecutor about the president's latest bid to shift the case from state court to federal court, where he could seek to have it dismissed on immunity grounds. There was no immediate decision.

The sides were in court for the second time in 11 days as Trump pursues a two-pronged legal strategy in an attempt to get the May 2024 verdict thrown out. Trump was convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to obscure a $130,000 payment to adult film performer Stormy Daniels.

Along with his federal court fight, the Republican president is also waging a traditional appeal through New York's state court system, which included arguments before the mid-level Appellate Division on Nov. 5. That court has yet to rule.

Regardless of the outcome, Trump will forever be associated with the case, which went to trial as he was campaigning for his return to the White House. Trump denies wrongdoing and was given no punishment. Now, with little over two years left in his presidency, he is steadfast in trying to rid himself of the dubious distinction of being the first U.S. president convicted of a crime.

Trump's lawyer, Robert Giuffra Jr., urged the 2nd Circuit judges on Monday to issue an order as soon as possible — even before writing their full decision — to take control of the case and stop the Appellate Division's deliberations.

Without federal court intervention, Trump "will likely have to wait years" for state appellate courts to rule before he can take the matter to the U.S. Supreme Court, Giuffra said in a letter previewing his argument.

national.title: Judge sets March retrial date for Lindsay Clancy in deaths of her 3 children
national.summary: A Massachusetts judge on Monday scheduled Lindsay Clancy's retrial for late March after prosecutors signaled that — at least for now — they intend to prosecute her again on first-degree murder charges in the killings of her three young children.
national.body:
Michael Casey, Associated Press Michael Casey, Associated Press

PLYMOUTH, Mass. (AP) — A Massachusetts judge on Monday scheduled Lindsay Clancy's retrial for late March after prosecutors signaled that — at least for now — they intend to prosecute her again on first-degree murder charges in the killings of her three young children.

Clancy's first trial ended in a mistrial after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was criminally responsible for the killings. Eleven jurors favored acquittal on the grounds of insanity, while one disagreed.

While the Plymouth County district attorney hasn't indicated publicly whether his office will pursue the same charges in a second trial, Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague told the judge during Monday's hearing that prosecutors were "ready to pick a jury trial date."

Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, said he took that to mean that prosecutors intended to go ahead with a first-degree murder case, as a lesser charge would allow Clancy to waive her right to have a jury.

"The die has been cast," Reddington told Judge William Sullivan. "I think you can read between the lines that when they say that the case is going to require a jury, that it's an indirect comment from the DA that they intend to proceed on first-degree murder indictments."

Prosecutors had sought a May trial date, citing scheduling conflicts, but Sullivan set the retrial for March 29.

The decision to schedule Clancy's second trial comes a week after Sullivan rejected a defense request to dismiss the charges. He ruled that a retrial would not violate Clancy's constitutional protection against double jeopardy.

national.summary: Pope Leo XIV bid farewell to his beloved second homeland of Peru on Monday with an "hasta luego," after a marathon 12-day South American tour that tested his stamina after lung cancer surgery.
national.body:
Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press

Astrid Suárez, Associated Press Astrid Suárez, Associated Press

Luis Andres Henao, Associated Press Luis Andres Henao, Associated Press

LIMA, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV bid farewell to his beloved second homeland of Peru on Monday with an "hasta luego," after a marathon 12-day South American tour that tested his stamina after lung cancer surgery.

During the traditional popemobile ride before Leo's final Mass, someone threw an apparent rosary toward the pope that seemed to hit him in the face. The pope winced and touched his temple, but he proceeded on and the Mass began as planned. The Vatican said some 1.5 million people attended.

The faithful often toss rosaries, stuffed animals, sports jerseys and other items towards the popemobile and Leo has often wowed the crowd with his quick reflexes in catching them. His bodyguards, though, have lamented that such tossed objects are among their chief concerns in protecting the pope when he is out in public.

For the Chicago-born Leo, who spent two decades in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop, the trip was an emotional homecoming to a place that he has credited with teaching him how to be a shepherd. Upon arrival, he declared that Peru was his "patria" or homeland, and he sang the national anthem alongside President Keiko Fujimori. Leo has American and Peruvian citizenship.

"It was here that you taught me how to be a bishop, and this time I learned a little more about serving as the Successor of Peter," Leo said at the end of Mass as many in the crowd knelt on the dirt ground to receive his final blessing.

national.title: BBC launches programme for children forced from school by bandits and poverty in West Africa

national.body:
As she pounds millet, 15-year-old Hadiza sings the English alphabet. It is a reminder of something that she desperately misses - going to school.

"Sometimes I write on the ground to practise and see if I'm still writing correctly," she says.

One night, about two years ago, a group of armed men raided her village.

"They scared our cattle away and abducted a girl. We had to run away. We walked barefoot all the way here," she says.

Since then she has lived in a displaced persons camp in Goronyo, a few kilometres from her home. For a short while she went to school here, but soon met a young man and, at the age of 13, stopped going to classes and got married.

"It's tradition here that once a girl is married, her education ends," she explains.

Now she lives with her in-laws and helps look after the home.

Although Nigerian law prohibits marriage under the age of 18, it is not always enforced.

national.summary: United Airlines said Monday that it had resolved a technology issue that delayed departing flights, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network prompted a nationwide ground stop.
national.body:
United Airlines said Monday that it had resolved a technology issue that delayed departing flights, just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration's network prompted a nationwide ground stop.

Chicago-based United said in a statement that while some flights were delayed because of the issue Monday afternoon, flights that were in the air and flights on its United Express regional network were not impacted. The airlines also said there was "no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue."

United apologized to customers for the inconvenience on social media. It resolved the issue about 1 1/2 hours after pilots first began reporting problems to air traffic controllers.

United did not immediately provide details about which of the airlines systems were affected, but pilots told air traffic controllers that the problem was related to United's system that helps them determine a plane's final weight to ensure it can safely take off.

A recording posted on the ATC app showed a United pilot in Houston asking the tower for permission to stay put at the gate until the system was working again. The app combines live air traffic control radio feeds with real-time visual aircraft tracking.

The flight tracking website FlightAware showed United with 418 delayed flights late Monday afternoon.

The United computer problem is just the latest high-profile technology meltdown in recent days.

Earlier Monday, thousands of people reported being unable to access their online accounts at several major U.S. banks after JPMorgan Chase had a technical problem.

national.body:
Bernard Condon, Associated Press Bernard Condon, Associated Press

President Donald Trump on Monday backed a long-shot bid to get Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, an extraordinary endorsement from a U.S. president given that his own intelligence agencies have reportedly determined Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy.

Trump suggested the ex-CEO of Nvidia could return, saying Huang "learned a big lesson" and he "would certainly not mind" if he was reinstated.

There's a "big group of people that would like him to return," Trump added.

The comments came as a "Stand with Jensen" petition set up last week gathered momentum, gaining signatures from current and former Nvidia staff, investors and other Silicon Valley supporters, including SpaceX boss Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, CEO of video game maker Epic Games.

The petition calls on the board to bring back Huang while an independent investigation proceeds or until there's "compelling evidence" that his departure is in the company's best interests.

"I'm signing it too," Musk posted on X, while Sweeney wrote, "Save Jensen!"

But in light of Huang's damaged reputation, China's chip threat and a pending Nvidia congressional probe, it's unclear that even a Trump-Musk endorsement will make a difference.

local.title: With burnout driving turnover, local leaders gather to tackle workplace mental health
local.summary: Rochester Regional Health's Dr. Brian Watkins will be speaking about a peer support group he developed for surgeons that is now operating system-wide.
local.body:
Burnout, defined as severe mental and physical exhaustion from prolonged stress, is a significant problem for both workers and their employers.

It can lead to employee disengagement and turnover. Some research says burned-out employees are three times as likely to leave their jobs than those who are more engaged at work.

Employee and workplace mental health is the theme of a one-day professional development conference in Rochester on Nov. 18 for human resources professionals, supervisors, and organizational leaders. The event will be presented by Eleversity, a professional training division of Heritage Christian Services.

Burnout is common among health care professionals. According to the American Medical Association, roughly 42% of physicians reported at least one symptom of burnout in 2025.

Dr. Brian Watkins, chair of surgery for the eastern region at Rochester Regional Health, will be speaking at the conference about Partners in Emotional Recovery, an employee peer support program he developed four years ago.

"Who are seen to be the most resilient, stoic, you know people within medicine? I think surgeons would be up on that list," Watkins said. '

Surgeons work in a high-stakes environment, making life-and-death decisions. And sometimes a patient dies after a procedure, or the doctor faces a complaint or a lawsuit.

"That's real stuff, and stuff that needs to be able to be spoken without fear of any consequence or retribution," Watkins said.

“Athletics will develop a district-wide team that brings together student athletes from across all high schools,” Rosser said. “This approach is intended to support consistent participation, coordinated training, and continued skill development."

Competitive cheer is a technical, skillful, and detail-oriented sport that involves choreographed routines with partner lifts, acrobatic tumbling, gymnastic stunts and human pyramids.

The decision to pull the sport from extracurricular offerings was in response to logistical challenges, safety concerns, and student participation, Rosser said. But critics pointed to the majority minority rosters of squads.

Participation during this past school year dropped from about 100 students at the start, to 60 students by the end of the program’s season, according to the district.

“If you’ve ever been to a cheer competition, just the diversity alone is so healthy for both sides, the rural, the suburban, and the city, and the charter [school students],” RCSD alumna Karen Iglesia of the non-profit Primetime585 said in a social media post Oct. 27. “The message we’re sending to these girls, especially these girls of color is that you’re just not worth it. You’re not worth the investment. … It’s wrong.”

Iglesia, who is an RCSD alumna and co-founder of Primetime585, which promotes youth sports and supports local athletes, called on the district in a Facebook video to keep competitive cheerleading intact.

local.body:
This past election I would say was a "once in a generation" event. The only other election as one-sided that I can remember was in 1964 when Barry Goldwater ran against Lyndon Johnson for President.

This past week was an election night to remember for Democrats, and they deserve credit for recruiting good candidates throughout the country. I suppose that some Democrats might believe that this crushing defeat for Republicans in the Congress represents a fundamental shift in our politics. Yet, I look upon it more as a vote against Trump, Trumpism, MAGA, and all that came with it.

The country realized that warrantless searches, the bashing of defenseless people by ICE, punitive tariffs, attacks on our traditional allies like Canada, and finally the military attack on Iran which resulted in the closing of the main sea artery for Mideast oil causing high energy prices--was essentially the work of one man--Donald J. Trump.

There was also a human dynamic, I believe, at work. Americans expect their Presidents to be reasonable, deliberate and undertake their duties with a sense of humility. I think President Trump's arrogance and lack of humility may have been the final straw in his undoing.

Since the country was going in the wrong direction, the only answer was to elect people to the House of Representatives and U.S. Senate who would stand up to all of this. Now, we have a branch of our government, the legislature (Congress,) elected to check the excesses of the current Executive and occupant of the White House.

I also believe that there was another issue which led to Trump's downfall and the licking that the Republicans took in the election…and that is the matter of elections themselves. Despite all of our bickering over politics, Americans remain pretty much united in believing in the sanctity of our elections. At its core, elections are the basis of our democracy.

When the Trump administration started going after our system of elections, getting the federal government and post office involved--that woke up a lot of people. It was clear that the intent of the White House was not to encourage voter participation but to suppress it.

It brought back memories of the President trying to subvert the 2020 election, the "patriots" storming the Capitol, phone calls to Georgia trying to find a few thousand more votes--all of that came into view again, and Americans were tired of it. Our system of elections works, and it should not be manipulated to help those who are in power.

The most recent Fredonia water boil order prompts the following thoughts. The October dry spell had lowered the reservoir water level so that organic matter was allowed to grow, overloading and disrupting the filtration system. When that matter clogged the system, high turbidity occurred.

Fredonia Village trustees are now faced with no options. The funds for the plan to draw down the reservoir do not exist. They cannot even meet the bill from LaBella, the engineering company they hired. Even if all the moneys and grants were in place, which they are not, it would take nearly five years to complete the hook up to Dunkirk's system.

Grants have been given to several surrounding communities. So, apply for the grants. The grants would give the village the money it needs to keep the current system running until another one is in place, so why even go to another system when the present one is already being updated?

There is but one path for the village of Fredonia to take. Start now to dredge the filtration end of the reservoir. A $5 million dollar grant would buy a lot of truckloads of dredged material.

Do partial dredging each year going forward. Deepen the reservoir while planting trees on its banks to keep soil and silt in place. And most importantly, develop a yearly maintenance plan going forward so future generations will have a clean, dependable source of water.

local.body:
It is with heavy hearts that we share that Samuel L. Drayo, Jr. peacefully passed away on November 11, 2026 at age 85.

Sam was a proud life-long resident of the Village of Fredonia. He was born December 27, 1940 in Dunkirk, NY. He graduated from the Fredonia Normal School (campus school at Old Main-kindergarten thru 8th grade) and Fredonia High School in 1958. He graduated from Syracuse University in 1962, where he earned a bachelor's degree in political science. He completed courses at the Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs. He was a 1965 graduate of Syracuse University College of Law earning a Juris Doctor degree.

Sam served two years in the U.S. Army from 1966-1968, attaining the rank of Captain. He was awarded the U.S. Army Certificate of Achievement and National Defense Service Medal. He received an honorable discharge in 1968.

In 1968, Sam joined his Dad, Samuel L. Drayo Sr., and twin brother, David C. Drayo, in his family's Fredonia law practice. Sam's son, John D. Drayo joined him in 2008 and they practiced together for many years. Sam served as Village Attorney for the Village of Fredonia for 47 years from 1969 to 2016 and Village Attorney for the Village of Brocton from 2005 to 2015.

In 1984, Sam helped organize the Northern Chautauqua County Youth Hockey Association (Dunkirk-Fredonia Steelers) and was its first President serving in that role for 8 years.

Sam was kind and had a generous nature and always found time to help others with legal and personal matters alike. He loved to laugh and had a great sense of humor. In his later years, Sam enjoyed researching, writing, and speaking about Fredonia historical and civic topics, frequently publishing pieces in The Observer. He also enjoyed traveling and made many trips to Italy with his life partner, Margaret C. Roberts.

He was a member of the Dunkirk-Fredonia Rotary Club, the Knights of Columbus, American Legion Post 59 and St. Anthony's Roman Catholic Church in Fredonia, N.Y.

Sam is survived by his loving partner, Margaret C. Roberts of Hamburg, NY (formerly Margaret C. Partridge) and his two sons, Michael (Kristie) Drayo of Phoenixville, PA and John Drayo of Fredonia, NY. He is also survived by three beloved grandchildren, Joshua Grant, Henry Drayo and Sadie Kathleen Drayo and former spouse, Susan R. (Meister) Star. He was predeceased by his twin brother, David C. Drayo who passed in 1985 and his parents, Samuel L. Drayo Sr. and Sadie (Mooradian) Drayo.

local.body:
The Fredonia Board of Trustees has moved its workshops to an hour before meetings and will no longer get together every Monday.

The Monday sessions alternated between workshops and meetings. The workshops are supposed to be for general discussion of village business with the meetings centered around resolutions that get voted on. The distinction matters little in Fredonia, where trustees will vote in workshops on items that they consider pressing.

Starting Nov. 23, the Fredonia trustees will now gather every other Monday in Village Hall at 5 p.m. for a workshop. The meetings are supposed to begin at 6 p.m. -- though when previous Fredonia boards had a similar schedule, the workshops often ran long.

The change comes after a recent workshop where Trustees LeeAnn Lazarony and Tim Mulholland questioned the need to convene every week. They feel village business can be successfully conducted without doing so.

Lazarony basically said she didn't want to be tied down every Monday, as she wants more flexibility to spend time with family out of state.

local.title: Is that old hunting ammunition still good?
local.summary: With New York’s Southern Zone regular big game firearms season opening this Saturday, hunters across Western New York are making their final preparations for deer season. But let’s be honest, each and every year — you know who you are, not everyone has enough time to get ready. Between demanding wor
local.body:
With New York’s Southern Zone regular big game firearms season opening this Saturday, hunters across Western New York are making their final preparations for deer season. But let’s be honest, each and every year -- you know who you are, not everyone has enough time to get ready.

Between demanding work schedules, sometimes working two jobs just to keep up with the cost of living, and the high taxes and expenses that come with living in New York, hunting preparations can easily get pushed to the back burner. For many, opening weekend is approaching faster than expected.

That brings up a familiar question: Have you ever wondered whether the ammunition you bought on sale 20 or 30 years ago is still viable? Is it safe to use? Will it perform the way it did when you first brought it home? Or, maybe, similarly, you’ve come across a few boxes in your dad’s gun locker after he passed away, or provided to you from the family of a friend. The ammo could be even older.

Perhaps you’re looking at your own firearm and ammunition storage collection and wondering why you bought 10 boxes of shotgun slugs when you typically use only one or two slugs each hunting season. Some years, you don’t use any at all.

It’s a familiar situation for many hunters. You're not alone. Ammunition can sit untouched for years, sometimes decades, between hunting seasons. The question is whether it has been stored properly and whether it’s still safe and reliable.

The best way to store hunting ammunition can vary by geographic location, but most scenarios require similar care. Western New York’s humid summers, cold winters and seasonal temperature swings make storage conditions especially important. Moisture, condensation and excessive heat are among the biggest enemies for ammunition. The golden rule: Keep ammunition cool, dry, protected from temperature swings and stored securely.

With rifle ammunition (centerfire hunting calibers), keep cartridges in their original factory boxes and place those boxes inside a quality, gasket-sealed ammunition container. This protects them from moisture and physical damage while preserving important caliber and lot information. A rechargeable or replaceable silica-gel desiccant can help control moisture. Avoid damp basements, unheated garages and storage areas subject to condensation.

With shotgun slugs, the same basic storage approach applies. Keep them in their original factory packaging, protected from moisture and physical damage. Pay particular attention to plastic hulls, crimps and any signs of cracking or deterioration.

local.title: Barker Lions shine a light on community service
local.summary: In 1927, Helen Keller came to the Lions International Convention and said, “The Opportunity I bring you, Lions, is this: To foster and sponsor the work of the American Foundation for the Blind. Will you not help me hasten the…
local.body:
Barker Lion Joel Strong, Barker President Jeff Jarvis and Therese Krull from Kax Solutions stuff envelopes.

In 1927, Helen Keller came to the Lions International Convention and said, “The Opportunity I bring you, Lions, is this: To foster and sponsor the work of the American Foundation for the Blind. Will you not help me hasten the day when there shall be no preventable blindness; no little deaf, blind child untaught; no blind man or woman unaided? I appeal to you, Lions, you who have your sight, your hearing; you who are strong and brave and kind. Will you not constitute yourselves Knights of the Blind in this crusade against darkness? I thank you.”

Since that time, Lions have sought to aid those who need. Barker Lions are proud to continue this work. During the past year, Barker Lions have aided members of our community by providing hearing aids, eye exams and glasses for those who cannot afford them. The group also built ramps at homes for those with physical challenges.

local.title: Three Buffalo Firefighters Injured, Child Rescued in Scoville Avenue Fire
local.summary: A fire on Scoville Avenue in Buffalo sent three firefighters to the hospital and left multiple residents displaced Monday afternoon.
local.body: A fire on Scoville Avenue in Buffalo sent three firefighters to the hospital and left multiple residents displaced Monday afternoon.The Buffalo Fire Department responded to 138 Scoville Avenue just after 3:30 p.m. Officials say two adults self-evacuated from the home, while firefighters rescued an 11-year-old girl.During the rescue, a firefighter became trapped on the second floor, prompting a Mayday call. Deputy Commissioner Paul Eason says crews experienced a loss of water pressure while searching for victims."It was a trapped situation when they went upstairs to look for the victims. And there was a cutoff or a loss of pressure from water. So they went and found a window and needed to be extricated out of the window," Eason said.Eason said crews were eventually able to get the trapped firefighter out safely."During that, one of our friends got trapped on the second floor. In the midst of that, they rescued three victims. Two of the parents self-extricated, rescued a little girl, 11-year-old girl. And one of our firefighters was trapped upstairs. They finally got him out," Eason said.Neighbor Judy Wray watched the scene unfold and described the moments as terrifying."It looked like the house was going to blow up or something, but it didn't, thank God," Wray said.WATCH: Three Buffalo Firefighters Injured, Child Rescued in Scoville Avenue FireWray also says she witnessed a firefighter fall from a ladder as crews tried to get out through a window."And then I seen a firefighter fall from the ladder. They were trying to get out of the window real fast. It was because it just all of a sudden got really flamed and then a big thing of black smoke. And the firefighter fell right off the top of the ladder and hit the ground. So that was terrifying," Wray said.The fire started on the first floor of the two-and-a-half-story home before spreading to the second floor and partially into the attic. A neighboring building at 142 Scoville Avenue also sustained damage.The Red Cross is assisting the affected residents, including two adults and two children from the upper residence and four adults and two children from the lower residence. Two adults from the lower residence suffered leg injuries while evacuating, and one child suffered smoke inhalation.Wray said her biggest concern is making sure everyone involved is okay."I just pray that they're going to be okay, you know.

local.title: SPCA Serving Erie County looking to ‘Pack the Pet Food Pantry’ ahead of holidays
local.summary: The SPCA Serving Erie County is asking the Western New York community to help stock its pet food pantry ahead of the holiday season.
local.body: The SPCA Serving Erie County is asking the Western New York community to help stock its pet food pantry ahead of the holiday season.The organization will hold its annual “Pack the Pet Food Pantry” event beginning Friday, November 20, with the goal of replenishing critical supplies used to help local pets and the families who care for them.The SPCA says its Pet Food Pantry provides more than 55,000 meals each month for local pets.Bethany Kloc, communications manager for the SPCA Serving Erie County, said the need has grown as families face rising costs.“It’s so needed because, as we all know, life has just been getting more and more expensive and people sadly are choosing between themselves, feeding themselves and their family, and feeding their pets,” Kloc said. “And anybody who has a pet knows that those pets are our family, and we don’t want anyone to go without.”WATCH: SPCA Serving Erie County looking to ‘Pack the Pet Food Pantry’ ahead of holidaysThe SPCA is asking the community to donate bags of dry dog and cat food, saying a little help can go a long way.Kloc said the organization is not looking for any particular brand, but donations should be unopened and unexpired.“We really need dry cat and dog food, unopened and unexpired,” Kloc said. “It doesn’t matter what brand. We are not picky. We just need the food.”SPCA Serving Erie County300 Harlem Road, West SenecaFriday, November 20: 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.Lumsden McCormick CPA369 Franklin Street, BuffaloFriday, November 20: 9 a.m. to noonAnderson’s Frozen Custard locationsFriday, November 20 through Sunday, November 22 during regular business hoursOnline donations are also being accepted.The “Pack the Pet Food Pantry” event is presented by Lumsden McCormick CPA.

local.body: North Tonawanda voters approved a property tax that will fund a brand-new community center for the city. entertainment.title: 5 TV Shows To Watch If You Like The Body
entertainment.summary: If you're one of the many people around the world loving Netflix's "The Body," here are five similar shows to add to your watchlist.
entertainment.body:
Netflix Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover "The Body" has hit a nerve with audiences around the world, reaching number one on Netflix's global chart shortly after its premiere in November. The show deftly blends teen drama with psychological horror elements to show the very real terrors of being a teenage girl. Created by Quinn Shephard, who also developed the Hulu hidden gem "Under the Bridge," the series follows a group of Catholic schoolgirls who are thrown into chaos when a member of their dance team falls into a coma.

With eight episodes in its first season, "The Body" makes for a quick binge. But once you tear through those episodes, what's next? If you're in the mood for more teen drama with a dark edge, we've got you covered. Shows set in the 1990s and 2000s are all the rage these days, so there's more where that came from, and YA horror never gets old, so this list dabbles in that genre, as well. If "The Body" is right up your alley, here are five more shows you should watch.

Showtime The Showtime series "Yellowjackets" is the perfect companion for "The Body." Both shows follow a close-knit group of teen girls faced with a series of horrific circumstances. In "Yellowjackets," our protagonists are a high school soccer team whose plane crash-lands in the wilderness. Trapped there with no prospect of rescue on the horizon, the girls must fight to survive, creating a feral, uniquely spiritual society in the wake of the disaster.

Like "The Body," "Yellowjackets" prominently features queer women and explores sexual awakening in the midst of its many horrors. The cast of the series is exceptional, and their chemistry is part of what makes "Yellowjackets" special. The interplay between the characters in the '90s crash timeline and the present day is fascinating, and the show does a brilliant job exploring the cost of survival. The '90s soundtrack brings an added touch of nostalgia, though the show never falls into the trap of putting the past on a pedestal.

Netflix "The Body" illustrates what happens when a tight-knit community with its own social rules is invaded by outsiders. Class is certainly relevant to the story, as Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros) and Leo (Jackson Kelly) come from a different background than most of their peers. In the Spanish series "Elite," which is sort of like a darker take on "Gossip Girl," social hierarchies are explored via juicy murder mysteries.

entertainment.summary: The production is the West End debut of playwright Rebecca Reid.
entertainment.body:
Hot on the heels of immense Oscar buzz for his latest outing in Martin McDonagh’s festival favorite Wild Horse Nine , the Academy Award nominee will co-star with Rosalind Eleazar in a production of Rebecca Reid’s History .

The play is set to mark Reid’s West End debut, and will have a limited run at Wyndham’s Theatre from May 17 to Aug. 7 2027. It follows Wren, who once had a vibrant, creative life until motherhood, sleepless nights and doomscrolling took over. On a reckless whim, she invites James — the ex who once defined her — to lunch. Their reunion forces Wren to reconsider a relationship she believed belonged firmly in the past. As the conversation unfolds, she discovers that the story she thought was finished may still be taking shape. “I couldn’t be more delighted to start work in the months to come on this fascinating new play, opposite Rosalind Eleazar and directed by Matthew Dunster,” Malkovich said. “I can’t wait. Rebecca Reid has written something rare — a play that is complex and profoundly human.” He was last on the London stage in 2019 with Bitter Wheat , David Mamet’s play inspired by the Harvey Weinstein scandal.

Malkovich has wowed audiences this year as a terminally ill CIA operative in the buddy-comedy Wild Horse Nine opposite Sam Rockwell. He’s also known for roles in Being John Malkovich , Dangerous Liaisons , and In the Line of Fire .

Eleazar, meanwhile, is a British star who most recently led Chris Rock’s Misty Green . She has a supporting role in Apple TV’s hit series Slow Horses and was the face of Netflix’s Harlan Coben adaptation Missing You .

entertainment.title: Quote Of The Day By Ted Danson: 'The Unspoken Message I Got As A Child Was...'
entertainment.summary: Cheers star Ted Danson shares what it was like growing up with very little money and how he now lives a life full of gratitude.
entertainment.body:
Younger TV fans may be more familiar with one of Danson's other hit TV shows . After a brief movie career that didn't stick, Danson returned to the small screen in sitcoms like 1996's "Ink" and 1998's "Becker." More recently, the white-haired actor has led series like "CSI: Crime Scene Investigation," "Bored to Death," "The Good Place," and "A Man on the Inside," which is set to wrap after its upcoming third season on Netflix . But while Danson has been in the spotlight for decades, he had to work hard to achieve that success. His perseverance is why he's today's quote of the day.

Static Media "The unspoken message I got as a child was that we had nothing. We didn't have TVs. I looked like a ragamuffin. My clothes were all hand-me-downs. My dad worked, and there was enough money for the necessities, but getting more and more money was never a goal."

The above quote comes from Ted Danson's 2017 interview with AARP . The actor was raised in Flagstaff, Arizona, where his father worked as an archeologist, anthropologist, teacher, and museum director.

In the interview, Danson discussed the ways anxieties over money and all the other "human stuff" still manifest in his life, occasionally in the form of physical issues. Danson is "a bit of a hypochondriac but in the most charming way," his wife, Mary Steenburgen, teased to the outlet. While Danson attributed a backache he was experiencing at the time to fear that he'll "never work again," Steenburgen cleared things up: "In all the years I've known him, the longest Ted's gone without a job was maybe 20 minutes."

Danson managed to elevate himself from a so-called "ragamuffin" to one of the most charming and charismatic actors on TV. While being anxious about money is part of being human, it's important to remember that finances aren't everything.

Now that Danson is more financially comfortable, he uses his money and time to support dozens of causes he's passionate about, including ocean conservation and oil policy reform. In recognition of his and Mary Steenburgen's philanthropic work, the Television Academy presented the couple with the prestigious Bob Hope Humanitarian Award in 2025. "[My father] taught me this life is not just about us. A lot of people have come before us, and a lot of people will come after us," Danson said in his acceptance speech. "It's about our stewardship of what we've been given."

entertainment.title: We Now Know What Robert Pattinson Was Doing When the James Bond Casting News Broke
entertainment.summary: All thanks to filmmaker Robert Eggers, who directed the star in 2019's 'The Lighthouse.'
entertainment.body:
The Hollywood Reporter heard from sources that the British star only found out he’d been tapped to succeed Daniel Craig as James Bond on Sunday morning, when Denis Villeneuve — who’s helming the next Bond movie — called him. Producer Amy Pascal was said to have informed the other candidates.

Within a day, the whole world knew too. Amazon MGM Studios, which bought the creative rights to the Bond franchise from producer siblings Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli last year, released the news via the character’s official social media accounts. Just before 7 a.m. PT on Monday, a tuxedo-wearing Pattinson emerged from the shadows, gun in hand. His announcement post has accrued over 1.2 million likes on X at the time of writing. Related Stories News Over 400 U.K. Industry Figures Demand End to "Culture of Open Secrets" After Russell Brand Trial Movies Tallinn Market Debates Estonia's Film Sector and How Foreign Shoots "Bring Both Value and Tension"

Thanks to Robert Eggers , who directed Pattinson in his 2019 period horror-fantasy The Lighthouse , we now know what the next Bond was up to when that news became public and sent the internet into a tailspin. During an on-camera interview with IGN , Eggers was asked if, while Pattinson’s character killed a seagull during the making of The Lighthouse , he ever stopped to consider: “There goes the next James Bond.”

“No, but I’m not surprised that it panned out the way that it did,” replied the Nosferatu filmmaker. “And also, crazily enough, he was watching a screening of Werwulf when the news broke, and I was just texting with him about it this morning,” he said, laughing.

Werwulf , set for release on Dec. 25 in the U.S., stars Eggers regulars Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Lily-Rose Depp, Willem Dafoe and Ralph Ineson, and is set to chronicle a cursed farmer’s transformation into a monstrous creature in 13th-century England. Coincidentally, Taylor-Johnson was among the rumored Bond contenders for a long time.

So what did our new Bond think of Werwulf ? “Oh, he loved it, of course,” added Eggers.

Pattinson, who this year alone has starred in The Drama , The Odyssey , Primetime and still has Dune 3 to come, said on Monday through an Amazon MGM Studios press release: “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime. I’m deeply grateful to Denis, Amy, David, Tanya and everyone at Amazon MGM Studios for their belief in me. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

entertainment.title: Music Victoria Goes Blunt in Election Fight for Music Funding
entertainment.summary: The peak body says dedicated state funding for Victorian artists falls to zero in 2027, with a live venue closing every 18 days.
entertainment.body:
Music Victoria has launched an election campaign calling on the next state government to legislate a 1% levy on ticket sales at stadiums, arenas and government-owned venues, warning that dedicated funding for Victorian artists and music creation drops to zero in 2027.

The Vote Victorian Music campaign, developed with creative agency Bolster, rolled out Tuesday (Nov. 17) across street posters, music venues and digital channels, using a profanity-laden slogan urging voters not to let politicians ruin “the music state.” Alongside it, the peak body published a scorecard grading each party’s commitments to the sector. Related CL Signs With THEBLACKLABEL, Reuniting With Longtime Producer Teddy For 'Full Circle' Moment Jeff Benjamin

The levy sits within a broader policy ask of roughly $114 million over four years. Proceeds would fund a permanent, independently governed Victorian Music Trust, which Music Victoria estimates would return about $4.4 million annually to the sector on top of government investment, insulating it from budget and election cycles. The organization says no party has committed dedicated funding beyond 2026.

“All sides of Victorian politics continue to underestimate music as a proven catalyst for wellbeing, community and social cohesion, and a multi-billion dollar driver of jobs, revenue and export,” chief executive Fiona Duncan said in a statement. “Our message is direct because the stakes are high.”

Victoria generates about a third of Australia’s music industry revenue — $3.55 billion annually and $1.28 billion in direct economic contribution, according to Creative Australia’s The Bass Line — and is home to the country’s largest concentration of independent record labels, 66% of its vinyl pressing capacity, half its independent record stores, 40% of its music managers and 31% of APRA AMCOS songwriters and publishers. Music Victoria says Melbourne alone has more record stores per capita than anywhere in the world.

At its pre-pandemic peak, according to the body’s Live Music Census, Melbourne had more live music venues per capita than London or New York, and Melburnians attended more gigs than AFL matches. A more recent audit of Music Victoria data by Live Music Locator found the state is now losing a live music venue every 18 days.

Public investment has not kept pace. Per-capita spending on music in Victoria has fallen to 63 cents, against $3.10 in New South Wales and $1.46 in South Australia, after more than a decade of flat baseline funding. Music Victoria says the impact extends beyond Melbourne, with regional venues, festivals and music businesses supporting local jobs in hospitality, tourism, events and production.

entertainment.title: Duetti Secures $665 Million Financing Round
entertainment.summary: The company's latest round includes an asset-backed securitization worth $450 million anchored by global investment firm Carlyle.
entertainment.body:
Catalog investment company Duetti has secured $665 million in financing following global investor Carlyle’s participation in its third asset-backed security (ABS) in two years, it announced Tuesday (Nov. 17).

The financing comes in the form of a $450 million ABS anchored by Carlyle, $165 million of additional credit from Duetti’s longtime bank, Viola Credit, and a $50 million side facility from Flexpoint Ford and Truist Bank. Flexpoint Ford is also an equity investor in Duetti.

Fast-growing Duetti has raised $1.3 billion since its launch in 2022 from equity investors like The Raine Group, Nyca Partners, Viola Ventures and ROC Nation, as well as from the debt markets. This securitization, worth more than three times Duetti’s last ABS of $125 million announced in January and issued with a higher rating, is a sign that institutional investors view Duetti as a maturing and stable business.

“We anchored this securitization because independent music royalties can generate the kind of recurring, diversified cash flows that asset-backed finance is built around,” Akhil Bansal , Carlyle’s head of asset-backed finance, said in a statement. “Duetti pairs industry expertise with the data and technology to build and manage catalogs at scale, and that’s what gives us conviction in the platform.”

Carlyle’s asset-backed finance team sits within its global credit platform, which has deployed more than $17 billion into the sports, media and entertainment sectors since 2017.

Duetti’s portfolio includes 50,000 master recordings and compositions by more than 3,000 recording artists, and the company continues to do around 80 transactions per month. The capital from this round of financing will be used to “significantly accelerate the pace and breadth of investment activities across genres and geographies, as well as different types of music rights,” the company said in a statement.

“Our third ABS transaction in just two years is more than five times the size of our inaugural deal in 2024, demonstrating our rapid growth, strong track record and increasing institutional demand for our catalog and business model,” Duetti CEO and co-founder Lior Tibon said in a statement.

Barclays, which handled both Duetti’s prior ABS transactions, led placement on this issuance.

Donald Trump blamed Joe Biden’s administration, while transportation secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin blamed old technology. Either way, late-night hosts had a field day with the news.

On Jimmy Kimmel Live , Jimmy Kimmel quipped, “Sometimes it feels like maybe Elon and his Doge bros shouldn’t have fired more than a thousand employees at the FAA.”

He added, “We learned this weekend a very valuable lesson. We learned what happens when the only experience your secretary of transportation has when it comes to transportation is being on Road Rules Allstars on MTV.”

On The Tonight Show , Jimmy Fallon also reflected on Trump’s decision to blame old FAA technology. “Today President Trump finally addressed the situation,” Fallon said before playing a clip of Trump telling reporters that the shutdown was caused by “very, very old equipment that had a heart attack.”

“In the times of crisis he really knows how to keep us calm,” Fallon noted. “Trump said the old equipment had a heart attack. And everyone watching that while flying also had a heart attack. Luckily there’s always a defibrillator nearby because that’s how they start the planes at Southwest.”
